title: Living on the Moon
summary: What people would need to live on the Moon: air, protection from heat, cold, dust, and radiation, and water from ice hidden near the south pole.
poll: People will live on the Moon in my lifetime.

versions.title: A Home on the Moon
versions.text:
Look up at the Moon at night. Could you live there one day? Some people think so.

The Moon is far from us. A trip there takes three days. Twelve men have walked on it. That was long ago.

The Moon has no air. You can not breathe there. An astronaut must wear a thick suit. A home on the Moon must be shut tight. It must keep air in.

The Moon has low gravity. Gravity is the pull that keeps us down. On the Moon, the pull is weak. You could jump six times as high!

It gets very hot in the day. It gets very cold at night. And one day there lasts two weeks.

The Moon has gray dust. It is sharp. It sticks to all things. It can hurt your lungs.

But there is ice in deep, dark holes near the south pole. Ice can be turned into water. It can help make air to breathe, too.

Now some lands plan to build a base there. A base is a place to live and work. In 2023, two Saudis went up to space. One day, a Saudi may go to the Moon, too!

versions.title: Living on the Moon
versions.text:
Look up at the Moon on a clear night. It seems close, but could human beings really live there one day? Many scientists believe they can.

The Moon is about 384,000 kilometers away. A trip there takes about three days. Only twelve people have ever walked on its surface, and the last ones came home in 1972.

The Moon has no air at all, which means you cannot breathe there, so an astronaut must wear a thick space suit. Any home built on the Moon must be sealed tightly to keep air inside.

The Moon also has low gravity. Gravity is the invisible pull that holds us to the ground, and on the Moon, this pull is only about one sixth as strong as on Earth. You could jump about six times as high!

In the daytime, the Moon becomes hotter than boiling water. At night, it becomes colder than any place on Earth. Each day and each night lasts about two weeks.

The ground is covered in fine gray dust. The dust is jagged, and it clings to suits and tools. Breathing it in could harm a person's lungs.

Still, there is good news. Scientists have found ice in deep, dark holes near the Moon's south pole. People could melt this ice for drinking water. They could also use it to make air to breathe.

Today, several countries are planning to build a base on the Moon. A base is a place where people can live and work for a long time. In 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to the International Space Station, so perhaps one day a Saudi will visit the Moon as well.

versions.title: Living on the Moon
versions.text:
Look up at the Moon on a clear night. It seems close, but could people really live there one day? Many scientists believe they can, and space agencies are already making plans.

The Moon is about 384,000 kilometers away, and a trip there takes about three days. Only twelve people have ever walked on its surface. The last of them came home in 1972.

The Moon has no air, so there is no oxygen to breathe. Outside, an astronaut must wear a spacesuit. Any home on the Moon must be sealed tightly to keep air inside.

The Moon also has low gravity, the pull that holds things to the ground. On the Moon, gravity is only about one sixth as strong as on Earth. You could jump about six times as high!

The temperature changes wildly. In sunlight, the ground can reach about 120 degrees Celsius, which is hotter than boiling water. At night, it can drop below minus 170 degrees. Each day and each night lasts about two weeks.

Without thick air, nothing blocks the harmful radiation that streams from the Sun and space. To stay safe, people may cover their homes with thick layers of moon soil.

The ground is covered in fine gray dust. It is sharp, it clings to everything, and it could harm a person's lungs.

Still, there is good news. Scientists have found ice in deep, dark craters near the Moon's south pole. People could melt it for drinking water and split it to make oxygen.

In 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to the International Space Station. Perhaps one day a Saudi will help build a base on the Moon.

versions.title: Living on the Moon
versions.text:
When you look up at the Moon on a clear night, it appears remarkably close, but could human beings genuinely live there one day? Many scientists believe they can, and several space agencies are already developing detailed plans for a permanent base where people could live and work.

The Moon is approximately 384,000 kilometers away, so a journey there takes about three days. Only twelve people have ever walked on its surface, all of them during NASA's Apollo missions, and the last of them returned home in 1972.

Because the Moon has no atmosphere, there is no oxygen to breathe. Outside the shelter, an astronaut must wear a pressurized spacesuit at all times, and any lunar home must be sealed tightly to prevent its air from escaping.

Furthermore, the Moon has low gravity, which is the force that holds objects to the ground. On the Moon, gravity is only about one sixth as strong as on Earth, so an astronaut could jump roughly six times as high.

The temperature changes dramatically, because in direct sunlight the ground can reach about 120 degrees Celsius, which is hotter than boiling water, while at night it can plunge below minus 170 degrees. Each lunar day and each lunar night lasts about two Earth weeks.

Without a thick atmosphere, nothing blocks the harmful radiation that streams from the Sun and from deep space. To protect themselves, settlers may cover their shelters with thick layers of moon soil.

The ground is covered in fine gray dust that is surprisingly sharp, and because it clings to equipment, it can wear out machines; it could also damage a person's lungs if it were inhaled.

Fortunately, there is encouraging news. Scientists have discovered ice in deep, permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's south pole. Settlers could melt the ice for drinking water and split it to produce oxygen.

In 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to the International Space Station. Perhaps one day a Saudi astronaut will help construct a base on the Moon.

versions.title: Living on the Moon: The Next Great Challenge
versions.text:
When you look up at the Moon on a clear night, it appears remarkably close, yet building a home there would be one of the greatest challenges in human history. Many scientists believe it is possible, and several space agencies are already developing plans for a permanent base where people could live and work.

The Moon is approximately 384,000 kilometers away, so a journey there takes about three days. Only twelve people have ever walked on its surface, all during NASA's Apollo missions, and the last of them returned home in 1972.

Because the Moon has no real atmosphere, there is no oxygen to breathe; outside, astronauts must wear pressurized spacesuits, and every lunar shelter must be sealed tightly so that its air cannot escape.

The Moon's gravity is only about one sixth as strong as Earth's, so an astronaut could jump roughly six times as high. Over long stays, however, weak gravity may weaken muscles and bones, so settlers would need to exercise every day.

Temperatures change dramatically. In direct sunlight the ground can reach about 120 degrees Celsius, while at night it can plunge below minus 170 degrees, and each lunar day and night lasts about two Earth weeks.

Without a thick atmosphere or a strong magnetic field, nothing protects the surface from the radiation that streams from the Sun and deep space. Settlers might therefore shield their shelters with thick layers of soil or build them inside underground tunnels.

The lunar soil, called regolith, is a fine gray dust with sharp, jagged grains. It clings to equipment, wears out machines, and could damage a person's lungs if inhaled.

Fortunately, the Moon also offers valuable resources. Scientists have detected ice in permanently shadowed craters in the polar region near the south pole. Settlers could melt it for drinking water and split it into hydrogen and oxygen for breathing and rocket fuel.

In 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to the International Space Station, and perhaps one day a Saudi astronaut will help construct a base on the Moon.

versions.title: Living on the Moon: The Next Great Challenge
versions.text:
When you gaze at the Moon on a clear night, it appears remarkably close, yet establishing a permanent home there would represent one of the most demanding challenges in human history. Many scientists consider the goal achievable, and several space agencies are already developing ambitious plans for a lunar base where people could live, work, and conduct scientific research.

The Moon is approximately 384,000 kilometers from Earth, which means that a journey there requires roughly three days, and only twelve people have ever walked on its surface, all of them during NASA's Apollo missions, and the last of them returned to Earth in 1972, more than fifty years ago.

Because the Moon has essentially no atmosphere, there is no oxygen to breathe; consequently, outside their shelters astronauts must wear pressurized spacesuits, and every lunar shelter must be sealed securely so that its precious air cannot leak into the surrounding vacuum.

The Moon's gravity is only about one sixth as strong as Earth's, which means an astronaut could jump roughly six times as high; during extended missions, however, reduced gravity may gradually weaken muscles and bones, so settlers would need to follow a disciplined exercise routine every day.

Temperatures fluctuate dramatically. In direct sunlight the ground can reach about 120 degrees Celsius, whereas at night it can plunge below minus 170 degrees, and because the Moon rotates slowly, each lunar day and night lasts approximately two Earth weeks.

Without a substantial atmosphere or a strong magnetic field, nothing protects the surface from the dangerous radiation that streams continuously from the Sun and from deep space, so settlers might therefore shield their shelters with thick layers of soil or construct them inside natural underground tunnels formed by ancient lava flows.

The lunar soil, called regolith, is a fine gray dust composed of sharp, jagged particles that were never smoothed by wind or water. Because it clings stubbornly to equipment, gradually erodes machinery, and could seriously injure a person's lungs if it were accidentally inhaled, engineers must design tools, suits, and filters that resist its damaging effects.

Fortunately, the Moon also offers valuable resources. Scientists have detected ice in permanently shadowed craters within the polar region surrounding the south pole. Settlers could melt this ice for drinking water and separate it into hydrogen and oxygen, which could supply breathable air as well as rocket fuel for further exploration.

In 2023, two Saudi astronauts traveled to the International Space Station, and perhaps one day a Saudi astronaut will help construct a permanent base on the Moon.

versions.title: Living on the Moon: The Next Great Challenge
versions.text:
The Moon lies approximately 384,000 kilometers from Earth, a distance that modern spacecraft can cross in roughly three days, yet despite decades of ambition, only twelve people have ever actually walked upon its surface, all of them during the Apollo missions, with the final crew returning home in 1972. Any future effort to establish a permanent lunar settlement will have to overcome a formidable combination of environmental obstacles.

Because the Moon has no atmosphere whatsoever, it offers no breathable oxygen and no natural protection from the vacuum of space, meaning that future settlers would need pressurized spacesuits for any excursion outside and carefully sealed shelters for everyday living. The Moon's gravity, roughly one-sixth that of Earth, would allow a person to jump about six times higher than on Earth, an exhilarating prospect, yet prolonged exposure to such weak gravity may gradually weaken human muscles and bones, making daily exercise routines an essential part of any long-term lunar life.

Temperature swings on the Moon are extreme: sunlit regions can reach roughly 120 degrees Celsius, while nighttime temperatures plunge below minus 170 degrees Celsius, and because each lunar day and each lunar night lasts about two Earth weeks, these punishing extremes persist for far longer stretches than anything experienced on Earth. Compounding the danger, the Moon's absence of both an atmosphere and a protective magnetic field leaves its surface almost entirely unshielded from harmful solar and cosmic radiation, a serious long-term health hazard for any permanent inhabitants.

To address this radiation problem, planners have proposed that settlers shield living quarters beneath thick layers of regolith, the fine, sharp, and jagged lunar soil that has never been smoothed or rounded by wind or flowing water the way Earth's soil has. This same regolith, troublesome as it is for equipment and potentially harmful if inhaled into human lungs, could nonetheless double as effective radiation shielding when piled over habitats. An alternative strategy involves constructing settlements inside naturally occurring underground lava tunnels, which would provide similar protection without requiring extensive excavation.

Among the Moon's most valuable resources is water ice, discovered hidden within permanently shadowed polar craters near the lunar south pole, regions so deeply shaded that sunlight never reaches their floors. This ice could eventually be melted for drinking water or split into hydrogen and oxygen, providing both breathable air and usable rocket fuel for future missions. In 2023, two Saudi astronauts flew to the International Space Station, a milestone that has fueled hope that a Saudi astronaut might one day contribute directly to the construction of humanity's first permanent Moon base.

versions.title: Living on the Moon: The Next Great Challenge
versions.text:
The Moon lies approximately 384,000 kilometers from Earth, a distance that modern spacecraft can traverse in roughly three days, yet despite decades of ambitious spaceflight, only twelve individuals have ever actually walked upon its surface, all during the Apollo program, with the final crew returning home in 1972. Any future effort to establish a genuinely permanent lunar settlement would need to overcome a formidable combination of interlocking environmental obstacles.

Because the Moon possesses no atmosphere whatsoever, it offers neither breathable oxygen nor any natural protection from the surrounding vacuum of space, meaning that prospective settlers would require pressurized spacesuits for every excursion beyond shelter and carefully sealed, airtight habitats for ordinary daily living. The Moon's gravitational pull, measuring roughly one-sixth of Earth's, would allow a person to leap approximately six times higher than on Earth, an exhilarating physical prospect, yet prolonged exposure to such diminished gravity may gradually weaken human muscles and bones over time, making rigorous daily exercise an essential, non-negotiable component of any sustained lunar existence.

Temperature fluctuations on the Moon are genuinely extreme: sunlit regions can reach approximately 120 degrees Celsius, while nighttime temperatures plunge to below minus 170 degrees Celsius, and because each lunar day and corresponding lunar night persists for roughly two full Earth weeks, these punishing thermal extremes endure for considerably longer stretches than anything experienced anywhere on Earth. Compounding this already severe danger, the Moon's simultaneous absence of both an atmosphere and a protective planetary magnetic field leaves its entire surface almost completely unshielded from harmful solar and cosmic radiation, posing a serious long-term health hazard to any would-be permanent inhabitants.

To address this persistent radiation problem, mission planners have proposed that future settlers shield their living quarters beneath thick accumulated layers of regolith, the fine, sharp, and jagged lunar soil that has never been smoothed, rounded, or weathered by wind or flowing water in the manner of ordinary terrestrial soil. This very same regolith, troublesome as it undeniably is for mechanical equipment and potentially hazardous if inhaled directly into human lungs, could nonetheless simultaneously function as effective radiation shielding when deliberately piled atop habitat structures. An alternative engineering strategy involves constructing settlements within naturally occurring underground lava tunnels, structures that would provide comparable protective benefits without necessitating extensive and costly excavation work.

Among the Moon's most scientifically and practically valuable resources is water ice, discovered concealed within permanently shadowed polar craters situated near the lunar south pole, regions so persistently shaded that direct sunlight never once reaches their crater floors. This frozen resource could eventually be melted to provide drinking water or chemically split into hydrogen and oxygen, simultaneously supplying breathable air and usable rocket propellant for future exploratory missions departing from a lunar base. In 2023, two Saudi astronauts successfully flew to the International Space Station, a historic milestone that has fueled considerable hope that a Saudi astronaut might one day contribute directly and meaningfully to the construction of humanity's first permanent lunar settlement.

questions.stem: Compared with Earth, what would be easier on the Moon?
options: Breathing outside without a suit
Staying safe from the dust
Jumping high
Keeping a steady temperature
questions.why: Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth as strong, so you could jump about six times as high.

wrong.A: There is no air to breathe on the Moon.
wrong.B: The dust is a danger on the Moon.
wrong.D: Temperatures change wildly on the Moon.

questions.stem: Why does the author end with the Saudi astronauts?
options: To show the trip takes three days
To connect space travel to readers in Saudi Arabia
To explain how spacesuits work
To prove people already live on the Moon
questions.why: Mentioning Saudi astronauts links the topic to readers' own country and future.

wrong.A: The trip length was explained earlier.
wrong.D: No one lives on the Moon yet.

MID.prompt: Choose the two biggest dangers of living on the Moon. Explain how people could deal with each one, using details from the article.
checklist: I named two dangers from the article.
I explained a solution for each one.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: One of the biggest dangers of living on the Moon is that there is no oxygen to breathe, so people would need to wear a spacesuit outside and keep their homes sealed tightly with air inside. Another danger is the wild swing in temperature, from scorching heat in sunlight to freezing cold at night, so a Moon base would need strong walls to handle both extremes. Settlers could also deal with harmful radiation by building near craters covered in thick layers of moon soil for protection.

keyWords.definition: the loose layer of dust and broken rock that covers the Moon
keyWords.example: The rover's wheels left deep tracks in the regolith.

keyWords.definition: energy that travels through space and can harm living cells
keyWords.example: Thick walls protect the hospital workers from radiation.

keyWords.definition: to protect something by covering it or blocking danger
keyWords.example: The tent will shield us from the hot afternoon sun.

keyWords.definition: useful supplies, such as water or materials, that people can use
keyWords.example: The town used its resources wisely during the dry summer.

keyWords.definition: near the North Pole or South Pole
keyWords.example: Polar bears live where the sea freezes in winter.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea?

options: They are made of broken glass from rockets
Settlers break them with tools
They were never smoothed by wind or water

questions.stem: Read this: "Settlers might therefore shield their shelters with thick layers of soil." What does shield mean?

As a comparison between Earth and Mars

HIGH.prompt: Imagine you are designing a Moon base. Explain where you would build it and how you would protect settlers from at least two dangers. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I chose a location and explained why.
I addressed at least two dangers with solutions from the article.
I used key words such as regolith, radiation, or shield correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I would build my Moon base near the polar region, close to the deep, dark craters where scientists have discovered ice, since that ice could be melted into drinking water and split into oxygen for the settlers. To protect against the harmful radiation that streams unblocked across the airless Moon, I would cover the base with thick layers of regolith, the fine moon soil, to act as a natural shield. I would also seal the base tightly against the wild day-and-night temperature swings, using these local resources to keep the settlers safe without needing to bring everything from Earth.
